cover.alt: A young player studies a fantasy game shop with virtual coins and outfits at a cozy desk.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Video games are fun, but they are also products made by people. Some games cost money before you play, while others are free to start. Both kinds need income to keep working. Their business choices can also affect how players spend real money.

items.prompt: What video game do you or your friends enjoy?
items.answer: Answers will be different. For example: My friends enjoy Roblox.

items.prompt: Have you seen a skin, pass, coin, or gem for sale in a game?
items.answer: Answers will be different. For example: I have seen character outfits for sale.

items.prompt: Why might a free game still need money?
items.answer: A free game still needs money to pay workers and keep the game running.

blocks.title: Part 1: A Game Is Also a Business
paragraphs: A game needs a team and technology. Programmers write code. Artists make characters and worlds. Other workers test the game, answer players, and fix problems. Online games also need computers called servers so people can play together.

A company can ask players to buy a game before playing. Another game can be free to start and sell extra things later. This is called free-to-play. Free-to-play does not mean the game has no business plan. The company still needs income to pay its costs and continue its work.

images.alt: One player buys a boxed game while another starts a free tablet game with an optional item shop.

items.prompt: Why does a free-to-play game still need income?
items.answer: It needs income to pay its workers and technology, fix problems, and keep the game running.
items.explanation: Which cost of making a game was new or surprising to you?

blocks.title: Part 2: Stores Inside Games
paragraphs: Many games have a store inside them. Official Fortnite information says players can use V-Bucks for Battle Passes, cosmetics, and other items. It also describes the Item Shop, outfits, and emotes. V-Bucks are a virtual currency used in Fortnite. Roblox has a Marketplace where users can find and buy items for a customizable avatar. Roblox creator information also explains purchases made with Robux.

A skin or outfit can make a character feel more personal. However, a digital item is not a physical toy that you can hold. Virtual currency can make the real cost less easy to notice, so it helps to check the price carefully.

images.alt: Arrows show money from a wallet changing into game coins and then a digital outfit.

items.prompt: What can players buy in the Fortnite store or the Roblox Marketplace?
items.answer: They can buy digital items such as outfits or clothes, and they can use virtual currency such as V-Bucks or Robux.
items.explanation: Which digital item would be useful or fun for you, if any?

blocks.title: Part 3: Passes, Subscriptions, and Ads
paragraphs: Games can earn money in several other ways. Roblox creator information describes passes that give a player a special privilege after one payment. It also describes subscriptions with a payment each month and immersive ads inside an experience. Fortnite documentation describes the Battle Pass as a way to unlock cosmetics, V-Bucks, and other items.

Rewarded ads are common in phone games. A player chooses to watch a short ad and receives coins or an extra life. The advertiser pays to show the ad, and part of that money goes to the game business. Together, these examples show how video games make money without charging every player in the same way.

items.prompt: How does a rewarded ad help both the player and the game business?
items.answer: The player gets a small game reward, and the business receives money from the advertiser.
items.explanation: Would you rather watch an ad or pay for a small reward? Why?

blocks.title: Part 4: Why Limited Things Feel Special
paragraphs: A game may run a limited-time event and offer a special character or item. The short time can make the item feel rare. Players may worry that they will miss their chance. This feeling is often called FOMO, or fear of missing out.

A timer tells you when an offer ends, but it does not mean you need the item. The item might return later, or it might not. Game companies use events to bring players back and show them new offers. A useful choice is to pause, check the real price, and decide after the first excitement becomes quieter.

images.alt: A young player pauses between a limited-time outfit and a savings jar before choosing.

items.prompt: Why can a limited-time item make someone want to spend money quickly?
items.answer: The player may feel FOMO and worry that the chance to get the item will soon disappear.
items.explanation: What could help a player slow down before buying?

blocks.title: Part 5: Updates and Smart Spending
paragraphs: New maps, characters, missions, and rewards give players a reason to return. When more people play for longer, they also have more chances to see a store or an ad. Updates can therefore support both the fun of a game and its business.

Before spending, set a budget and ask a few questions. Do I really want this, or am I reacting to FOMO? Will I use this pass often? What else could I buy with the same real money? A child can also ask a parent or another trusted adult. A skin may be worth it to one player and not worth it to another.

items.prompt: What are two questions a player can ask before spending money in a game?
items.answer: A player can ask whether they truly want the item and whether they will use it often.
items.explanation: Which spending question is most helpful for you?

items.prompt: Is buying a skin worth it? Use ideas from the lesson to explain your opinion.
items.answer: There is no single answer. A skin may feel worth buying when it fits your budget and you truly enjoy it. It may not be worth buying when you only feel pressure from FOMO or will not use it often.
